messages.author: bd1e86fc1630832f
messages.subject: Speeding up a hierarchical model
parts:
I would like to use a hierarchical model to jointly estimate
parameters for about 200 groups, each with about 30 datapoints. I've
tried a number of formulations (using fewer parameters that vary by
group, using normal distributions rather something more dispersed,
having more or fewer priors and hyperpriors), but I cannot get Stan
(I'm using rstan) to produce a result in fewer than about 20 hours
(and my preferred formulation would take much longer).

Below is my code (one of the "preferred" versions). Do you have any
suggestions for speeding this up by an order of magnitude or two? The
number of datapoints is not consistent across the groups.

data {
int<lower=0> N; // datapoints
int<lower=0> M; // groups
// the data
real yy[N];
real<lower=0> xx[N];
real zz1[N];
real zz2[N];
// group identifier
int<lower=0> group[N];
}
parameters {
// parameter of interest
real beta;

// group parameters
real alpha[M];
real gamma1[M];
real gamma2[M];
real<lower=0> sigma2[M];
real<lower=1> nu;

// hyperparameters
real mu_alpha;
real<lower=0> sigma2_alpha;
real mu_gamma[2];
real<lower=0> sigma2_gamma[2];
real<lower=0> nu_sigma2;
real<lower=0> s_sigma2;
}
model {
// priors
alpha ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma2_alpha);
gamma1 ~ normal(mu_gamma[1], sigma2_gamma[1]);
gamma2 ~ normal(mu_gamma[2], sigma2_gamma[2]);
for (m in 1:M)
sigma2[m] ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(nu_sigma2, s_sigma2);
1 / nu ~ uniform(0, 1);

// core model
for (n in 1:N)
yy[n] ~ student_t(nu, alpha[group[n]] + beta * xx[n] +
gamma1[group[n]] * zz1[n] + gamma2[group[n]] * zz2[n],
sigma2[group[n]]);
}

Thanks for any suggestions!

- James

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Speeding up a hierarchical model
parts: On Tuesday, April 30, 2013 10:00:46 PM UTC-4, jrising wrote:

Below is my code (one of the "preferred" versions).  Do you have any
suggestions for speeding this up by an order of magnitude or two?

model {
    // priors
    alpha ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma2_alpha);
    gamma1 ~ normal(mu_gamma[1], sigma2_gamma[1]);
    gamma2 ~ normal(mu_gamma[2], sigma2_gamma[2]);
    for (m in 1:M)
      sigma2[m] ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(nu_sigma2, s_sigma2);

This won't make a huge difference but I think you can just do (without an explicit loop)

sigma2 ~ scaled_inv_chi_square(nu_sigma2, s_sigma2);
Here you need to manually adjust lp__ for the change-of-variables.

// core model
    for (n in 1:N)
      yy[n] ~ student_t(nu, alpha[group[n]] + beta * xx[n] +
        gamma1[group[n]] * zz1[n] + gamma2[group[n]] * zz2[n],
        sigma2[group[n]]);
  }

This is probably the only place where you can get a appreciable speedup. If you declare a vector[N] called location and another vector[N] called scale at the top of the model block and do

for(n in 1:N) {
  location[n] <- alpha[group[n]] + beta * xx[n] + gamma1[group[n]] * zz1[n] + gamma2[group[n]] * zz2[n];  
  scale[n] <- sigma2[group[n]];
}
y ~ student_t(nu, location, scale);

it will go faster.

Ben
